title: My Five Predictions On AI For IT In 2024
text: Elise Carmichael is the CTO of Lakeside Software, where she oversees the design and delivery of its digital employee experience platform.   It’s been a little more than a year since OpenAI launched ChatGPT using the GPT 3.5 large language model (LLM), forever disrupting business as usual everywhere. Even though generative AI is very exciting for long-time computer science folks like me, it will take many organizations a while to get comfortable with using and/or building custom GenAI models and, more importantly, to trust them. It is easy to trust a chatbot that seems to give credible answers, but these models are really just figuring out what the next word in a series should be. Although they are scarily accurate, they are known at times to “hallucinate” (15%-20% of the time in the case of the latest ChatGPT model). One infamous example: “Some species of dinosaurs even developed primitive forms of art, such as engravings on stones.” Regardless, we can’t live in the dinosaur age of technology (a.k.a. the era from, say, the wheel to November 29, 2022). In fact, we’ve all heard that “AI is eating the world.” We don’t need to fear it; however, instead, why not grab a spoon and dig in? Only then can a company claim a primo seat at AI’s table, relishing its business benefits if the AI recipe is right. In my world as the CTO of a software company that serves the IT community, from CIOs trying to mitigate digital risk to IT practitioners trying to deliver a better digital experience, I have five of my own predictions about AI for IT in 2024. Although the kind of AI models I envision may not be as cute as Disney Research robots (my husband helped build this one!), I still find them to be pretty darn fascinating. One of the biggest issues with LLMs comes down to trust. Whether you’re integrating existing LLMs or building your own (which only the largest enterprises are likely to do as I discussed with Zack Kass, formerly of OpenAI), can you and your customers trust the model to give you right and relevant answers? Explainability is a problem that most product companies have when implementing machine learning algorithms. If you’re making business decisions off the GenAI model, it must be incredibly trustworthy. How do you get around the hallucinations? Well, you keep the “human in the loop” to validate as you go. Let’s say you want to query a large dataset, so you prompt, “Show me all employees and their corresponding time zones.” You want to ensure that the response is labeled and know exactly where it comes from. If there is a business decision to be made, the model’s output must be accurate. AI without human oversight in applications is dangerous where the right level of trust has not been established. Let’s face it: Early-career employees have grown up with iPhones and laptops that just work. The digital employee experience of these employees is simply not the same as that of the generation that grew up with less sophisticated devices that required regular troubleshooting. Given that IT teams have to strategically accommodate these two different levels of experience in the workforce at the same time, I think that IT teams are going to look to GenAI to serve up quick answers or automated self-service options—with AI as an easy button of sorts. If IT cannot accommodate easy fixes, digital natives are going to get frustrated very fast when their unfamiliar operating system is “running slowly.” It’s important to acknowledge, too, that being on the phone for IT support is the last thing early-career employees are expecting. That vision is as outdated as a landline phone, so IT teams will want to mature their automation and AI capabilities for faster responses and simpler self-help options. There has been this giant move from on-premise data centers to everything cloud. Because the cloud is very expensive, however, I foresee that more and more companies will turn to the edge, even for training foundational AI models. Not every company has a partnership with Microsoft/Google/AWS to get reduced-price compute power, but every company has an army of compute that mostly sits idle at night. My prediction is that we will see a move toward the distributed edge network for compute power. I personally think that, because of GenAI, the world will be unrecognizable in 10 years in terms of tools and technology—with a big impact on how users work with computers and services. We may start to see the first fissures of a chasm between the early AI adopters and the late adopters. Remember the nearly 20-year-old theory of “disruptive innovation” by Clayton Christensen, Michael Raynor and Rory McDonald? Gee, I wonder what Blockbuster thought about that? With GenAI gaining a steady foothold, we will face another wiping out of corporate mastodons if they don’t start innovating (today) and delivering (tomorrow) on all the possibilities of GenAI. LLMs aren’t new, but how fast and accurate the models are is new–-even when it’s coming up with new content (zero-shot learning, or “the ability for AI to learn to do new tasks without any training”). Data is the main driving factor, making the latest models “scarily” accurate! They often create new, accurate content without ever having seen it in the wild. So, my prediction for this year (and well beyond) is that data will be the name of the GenAI game. As my company’s CEO Dave Keil recently wrote, “The real breakthrough of generative AI is the data itself.” Indeed, the better the data, the better the AI. That said, I think that companies with the deepest data lakes for their given industry will win the AI long game. Since my company has been collecting IT endpoint data for more than 25 years, I certainly hope so! Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

As the CTO of a software company serving the IT community, I have been closely observing the advancements in AI and its potential impact on the IT industry. With AI technologies evolving rapidly, I have come up with five predictions for AI in IT in the year 2024.

1. Trust in AI Models:
AI models, particularly generative language models, have gained immense popularity but also raised concerns about their trustworthiness. While these models can provide accurate responses, they can sometimes "hallucinate" and generate incorrect information. To overcome this challenge, businesses integrating these models must establish a human validation process to ensure the accuracy of the output. Trust and explainability are critical for leveraging AI effectively.

2. GenAI for Digital Employee Experience:
The digital employee experience is rapidly changing as younger generations, accustomed to sophisticated devices, enter the workforce. IT teams will increasingly rely on AI-powered solutions, such as automated self-service options and quick answers, to cater to the varying levels of technical expertise among employees. As IT departments strive to enhance user satisfaction, AI will be leveraged as an "easy button" for quick resolutions.

3. The Edge Computing Shift:
With the significant migration from on-premise data centers to the cloud, companies are facing increased costs. In response, more organizations will turn to edge computing and distributed networks to leverage their existing idle compute resources efficiently. Even foundational AI models' training will likely occur on the edge, making use of readily available compute power without the need for costly cloud partnerships.

4. Widening Gap Between AI Early Adopters and Late Adopters:
As AI continues to evolve, there will be a growing divide between companies that embrace AI innovations and those that lag behind. Just like the disruption caused by technologies like streaming services to traditional video rental stores, organizations failing to invest in and leverage AI may face significant setbacks. GenAI's possibilities require companies to innovate and deliver on its potential to stay competitive.

5. The Power of Data:
The driving force behind AI is high-quality data. The more accurate and relevant the data, the better the AI models perform. In 2024, companies with deep data lakes specific to their industries will hold a competitive edge. Those with extensive data collection and analysis capabilities will be well-positioned to excel in the AI landscape. The breakthrough in generative AI lies in the data itself.

In conclusion, AI's impact on the IT industry is set to grow exponentially in 2024. Trustworthy AI models, personalized employee experiences, edge computing, and data-driven strategies will play pivotal roles in shaping the future of IT. The challenge lies in embracing these changes while staying ahead of the competition, ensuring innovation and adaptability become cornerstones of success.

It’s no secret that technology is constantly evolving and improving, and smartphones are no exception. In fact, according to experts at Gartner, we can expect a surge in the development of GenAI smartphones in the near future. But what exactly does this mean for the average smartphone user?

GenAI, short for General Artificial Intelligence, refers to the integration of advanced AI capabilities within smartphones. This includes enhancements in voice integration and camera functionality, which have become increasingly important to users. However, it's not just about these improvements alone. Gartner emphasizes that the availability of innovative apps that make use of GenAI capabilities will be crucial in driving the demand and adoption of these smartphones.

With the help of GenAI, smartphones will become even more intuitive companions, capable of understanding and responding to human language and visual cues. By leveraging large language models created specifically for smartphones, the overall user experience will be elevated to new heights. Imagine a smartphone that can interpret your commands, understand your intentions, and deliver personalized recommendations tailor-made to your preferences.

In the current market, we can already see examples of GenAI technology in action. Google's Gemini Nano, Baidu's Ernie, and Open AI's GPT-4 are just a few examples of the AI models that are being integrated into smartphones to enhance their capabilities. These models enable smartphones to process, interpret, and respond to information more intelligently, making them much more than just devices for communication and entertainment.

According to Gartner's projections, the number of smartphones with GenAI capabilities is expected to reach a staggering 240 million units this year alone. This significant increase from practically none in 2023 demonstrates the rapid pace at which this technology is being adopted and integrated into smartphones.

Interestingly, Gartner also notes that smartphone shipments started to increase again in the fourth quarter of 2023 after a prolonged decline. It is anticipated that shipments will continue to grow by 4.2%, reaching 1.2 billion units this year. However, analysts caution that this growth may not necessarily indicate a complete recovery for the smartphone market.

The future of GenAI smartphones looks promising, and it's an exciting time for technology enthusiasts. As these devices continue to evolve and become more advanced, we can expect a whole new realm of possibilities and applications. From enhanced voice assistants to improved photography capabilities, smartphones are set to become smarter and more responsive than ever before.

In conclusion, the surge in GenAI smartphones brings forth a wave of innovation and potential for improved user experiences. With advancements in AI technology and the integration of sophisticated language models, smartphones are transforming into intelligent companions that can understand and cater to our needs. As we embrace this era of GenAI smartphones, the possibilities for enhanced productivity, entertainment, and convenience are endless.

Introduction:

While this advancement in technology is exciting, Gartner also explained that it will not have a significant impact on overall smartphone demand until 2027. This article will delve into Gartner's predictions, shedding light on the potential of GenAI technology in smartphones.

The Current State of GenAI on Smartphones:
According to Gartner, current GenAI technology enhances various functions, such as camera capabilities and voice integration. While users appreciate these updates, they are unlikely to pay a premium for GenAI-equipped smartphones without the availability of groundbreaking applications. This suggests that market demand will take time to catch up with the advancements being made in GenAI technology.

The Catalyst for a Shift in User Experience:
Gartner believes that the real game-changer in smartphone user experience will be the development of large language models specifically designed for smartphones. These models will transform smartphones into highly intuitive companions that can understand and respond to human language and visual cues, thereby elevating the overall user experience to unprecedented heights. Notable examples of GenAI technology currently featured on smartphones include Google's Gemini Nano, Baidu's Ernie, and Open AI's GPT-4.

Gartner's projections indicate that approximately 240 million GenAI-equipped smartphones will be shipped this year, compared to almost none in 2023. This staggering growth reflects the increasing adoption and integration of GenAI technology across the smartphone industry. However, it is crucial to note that Gartner expects a full-fledged recovery and substantial impact on consumer demand to occur closer to 2027.

After nine consecutive quarters of decline, Gartner reports that smartphone shipments made a comeback in Q4 of 2023. The organization predicts a 4.2 percent increase in shipments to reach 1.2 billion units in 2024. However, it is important to remain cautious, as this recovery might not necessarily indicate a complete rebound in the market.

GenAI technology has the potential to revolutionize the smartphone industry, enhancing user experiences and making smartphones more intuitive than ever before.
